agreement.description: Gary Kildall and Dorothy McEwen establish and independently manage Digital Research. Adam supplies minority investment and strategic cooperation to support a new approach to personal computing compatible with CP/M. DRI retains CP/M ownership and its independent licensing business. Gary and Dorothy may buy back Adam’s shares at any time at a price assessed by an independent valuation agency.

clauses.statement: Adam receives a 30% fully diluted minority interest in DRI for his capital commitment and founding contribution. This stake supports his plan for a new approach to personal computing compatible with CP/M; it does not give him day-to-day control of DRI.
clauses.unit: percent of DRI fully diluted shares

clauses.statement: DRI reserves 10% of its fully diluted equity for future employees. The reserve is unallocated and is not an issued voting block.
clauses.unit: percent of DRI fully diluted shares

clauses.statement: Adam commits USD 250,000 in nominal 1974 money over two years: USD 150,000 at formation and USD 100,000 in scheduled instalments. This funds DRI’s business and does not purchase CP/M ownership.

Gary and Dorothy manage DRI independently. Transactions with Logix receive independent review, and DRI remains free to serve other manufacturers. Expansion cards and chip licensing remain Logix and AION responsibilities.
Gary leads DRI’s engineering and CP/M technical development as an independent co-founder.
Dorothy leads DRI’s operations and business administration as an independent co-founder.

Adam supplies the agreed capital, strategic advice and OEM relationships as a minority investor. He supports collaboration with Logix while respecting Gary and Dorothy’s independent management and DRI’s CP/M ownership.
Gary Kildall and Dorothy McEwen have the right to buy back Adam’s DRI shares at any time. The purchase price is assessed by an independent valuation agency when the right is exercised.

agreement.title: Logix–DRI–AION CP/M, TUI and developer-platform agreement

party.role: Aurelia platform partner and development collaborator
CP/M developer, sole software owner and licensor
negotiator for the Logix collaboration
TUI developer and source-delivery partner; owner and developer of AION C IDE

agreement.description: Logix, DRI and AION Software agree the Aurelia operating-system and developer platform. DRI develops the CP/M extensions and integrates the TUI implementation delivered by AION. Logix supplies hardware, boot firmware and low-level drivers; AION Labs supplies qualified ROM chips to Logix requirements. AION develops and owns the separate AION C IDE. The January 1975 agreement establishes development obligations; integration and qualification precede the June 1978 launch.

clauses.statement: DRI retains the right to implement the TUI libraries and FlexiBUS support in CP/M versions for non-Logix computers.

DRI leads CP/M command/file services, operating-system memory and cartridge runtime, shared clipboard storage and bounded I/O scheduling. Logix supplies hardware requirements, boot/recovery firmware, initial mapping and low-level drivers. AION Software develops the TUI and the separate C development environment. Logix leads complete-system acceptance with DRI and AION component qualification.

DRI owns the resulting CP/M version, its CP/M enhancements and the accepted CP/M TUI implementation delivered by AION, with source, documentation and tests. DRI may maintain, modify and license these implementations non-exclusively for other hosts. AION retains its compiler/IDE and pre-existing general-purpose components; any such components included in the delivery carry perpetual rights for DRI to maintain, modify and redistribute them with CP/M. Hardware ownership is not transferred.

AION Software designs and implements the shared text-mode TUI API, controls, editing, menus, forms, lists and pseudo-windows, with C bindings and assembly implementations where appropriate. DRI accepts the source and tests and integrates the implementation into the CP/M system cartridge. Mutable state remains in reserved RAM; applications call shared services rather than embedding another full TUI library.
Support smart devices and expansion cards using Plug and Execute and FlexiBUS technologies, with documented CP/M integration so qualified devices and cards can expose their functions to applications.

DRI adapts CP/M and suitable cartridge code for XIP, separating ROM code/constants from RAM state. Logix supplies mapping hardware and safe boot primitives. Define image headers, entry points, relocation assumptions, RAM initialization, nested calls, callbacks and recovery. Arbitrary existing CP/M binaries are not automatically ROM-executable.

DRI implements user-area support and named groups as explicit extensions to the CP/M 1.4-derived release. Names map to CP/M User Numbers; they do not create hierarchical directories. DRI specifies persistent name metadata, valid names, default selection, enumeration, rename behaviour and compatibility with ordinary CP/M tools before interface freeze.

Logix, DRI and AION jointly maintain the published TUI interface specification. AION retains perpetual rights to reuse, modify and port the delivered TUI source and shared technology for other operating systems and processors, including non-CP/M targets. DRI retains independent CP/M licensing; later improvements require documented compatibility and contribution terms rather than an implied transfer of unrelated software.

DRI owns operating-system bank and cartridge dispatch, preserves caller mappings and stacks, and handles nested calls, interrupts and page-crossing buffers. Stable common-memory code and the system stack remain accessible. Logix owns reset mapping, hardware primitives and controller timing/refresh/DMA behaviour. Installed RAM is distinct from the writable application area advertised before launch; no service silently reduces a running application's TPA.

Logix supplies hardware video drivers and monitor capability discovery. DRI integrates mode selection and supported display services into CP/M, rejecting unsupported configurations. AION implements adaptive TUI layout and rendering over those services, without assuming fixed video addresses or universal 80-column support.

DRI provides clipboard storage/lifecycle and a bounded I/O request service. AION and DRI define clipboard formats and copy/cut/paste semantics. Clipboard and I/O buffers have separate lifetimes and ownership. Define bounds, overflow, persistence, per-device ordering, completion, cancellation, timeouts, errors and flushing; slow devices must not block keyboard service. Standard CP/M calls retain synchronous semantics; this does not introduce foreground multitasking.

Logix owns hardware and cartridge electrical design, address decode and ROM capacity/timing requirements. AION Labs implements and manufactures qualified ROM chips to those requirements under Logix supply arrangements. DRI releases the integrated CP/M image after accepting AION TUI source; Logix controls production image revisions, programming/mask handover and verification with AION Labs. Semiconductor manufacture transfers no software rights.

AION Software develops and owns AION C IDE for Aurelia: integrated editor/build workflow, Z80 C compiler and optimizer, assembler/linker, runtime libraries, TUI bindings, diagnostics, debugging and disk/XIP image tools. The IDE is a separately distributed disk-based offering; the reusable TUI runtime is supplied in the CP/M system cartridge. DRI supplies stable OS interfaces and integration assistance.

Agree interface and calling-convention freezes, source/test/documentation handovers, component acceptance and complete-system qualification before the June 1978 release. DRI funds/staffs its OS work, AION its TUI/IDE work and Logix its platform/integration work, subject to separately documented commercial arrangements. Assign defect ownership by component and jointly triage integration faults. Measure ROM images, stacks, buffers and application RAM; publish supported configurations and replacement/patch procedures. No date alone proves acceptance or manufacturing readiness.

agreement.description: BPI Systems accepts Adam’s $150,000 investment in exchange for a 33% fully diluted interest. The agreement obliges AION Software to provide knowledge and resources to refactor BPI’s existing code into C with a competitive text-mode TUI. Further investment supports ports to future systems and platforms, after which BPI has the right to buy back Adam’s shares. The same agreement covers BPI’s operating independence, distribution, specialist support and authorised training. Logix and the Academy provide distribution, hardware support and training services.

clauses.statement: Adam agrees to subscribe $150,000 of new capital into BPI Systems for development and working capital. BPI accepts the subscription; it is company funding rather than a payment to existing owners.

The accepted investment agreement allocates Adam a 33% fully diluted interest in BPI Systems in exchange for his $150,000 subscription. Existing owners retain the remaining 67%, subject to the agreed later buyback right.
clauses.unit: percent of BPI fully diluted shares

clauses.statement: AION Software must provide the knowledge, engineering resources and development assistance needed to refactor BPI’s current code into C and deliver a competitive TUI with pseudo-window interaction in text mode. BPI retains ownership of its applications and its independent brand and management.

The cooperation includes further investment and engineering work to port the refactored BPI software to future systems and platforms. AION Software supplies the associated technical knowledge and resources. Additional funding amounts, allocation among contributors, target platforms and schedules remain unspecified.

Following the agreed redevelopment and subsequent porting work, BPI Systems may buy back Adam’s shares. This is BPI’s right, not an automatic transfer or a mandatory buyback. The agreement does not specify a price, valuation formula, exercise date or payment schedule.

BPI retained its management, brand, application ownership, licensing and specialist support. AION Software provided engineering assistance and Logix provided distribution and training. Operational cooperation implements the accepted investment and C/TUI redevelopment agreement while preserving BPI’s operating independence.

BPI owned its applications and managed licensing, updates and specialist support. AION Software supplied engineering assistance, while Logix distributed the products and supported the hardware. Dealers handled installation enquiries. Public presentations described this commercial partnership and identified Adam’s accepted investment and the C/TUI redevelopment partnership.

Academy begins BPI-authorised practical courses and direct distribution under a cooperation agreement. Dealers handle first-line installation enquiries, BPI handles software defects and specialist support, and Logix supports hardware. Tuition, setup services and software licences remain separate.

AION Labs and SMC prioritised the transfer of monitor controllers and controllers for FlexiBUS peripherals, supporting independent monitor and peripheral manufacturers. The wider licence scope remained available for other custom chips outside the ERA processor family.

agreement.description: Adam signed the January development agreement for Logix, with John Walker representing Autodesk’s organising founders. Autodesk adopted the arrangement after incorporation in April. Logix sponsored development and supplied hardware, distribution and joint marketing; Autodesk retained ownership of its software and its cross-platform business.

clauses.statement: Non-exclusive funded development. Autodesk retains its software ownership and cross-platform business; clear the underlying Interact contribution/porting rights with the founders, including Mike Riddle. Logix supplies distribution and joint marketing, without a source buyout or forced platform exclusivity.

Adam commits the staffing, equipment, licences and integration resources required by the agreed delivery plan. Procurement and staffing are reviewed against the November 1982 delivery objective; the agreement specifies no fixed dollar ceiling.

Autodesk undertook to deliver a release-quality Artemis/AIONix build of AutoCAD 1.0 for the joint November 1982 COMDEX presentation. Commercial deliveries followed acceptance of the agreed drawing, exchange, plotting and recovery tests.

Logix supplies each assigned developer with an Artemis PRO workstation with 1 MiB RAM, local storage and an available display, plus shared build and test machines and spares required by the agreed staffing plan.

Install the entire AION Development System — Team Edition: C Development Environment 2, ERA compiler/linker/debugger and validated floating-point math library; source repository, branches/reviews, tasks, collaboration, reproducible builds, release labels and target testing.

Supply network adapters, hub, cabling, configured accounts and project permissions, and dedicated Artemis PRO server capacity. Scale sponsored server/license deployments to the whole team within qualified concurrency; the retail four-session entitlement is not silently unlimited.

The standard 5 MB disk is inadequate as a presumed whole-team repository/build archive. Fund and qualify larger storage, additional volumes/servers, independent backup media, restore tests and off-machine source archives; capacities follow measured source/build/history budgets.

Fund dedicated Autodesk engineering time, AION compiler/runtime and integration specialists, installation, training, documentation, replacement hardware, plotter access and on-site support through release. Retail onboarding/support-hour caps do not limit this separately sponsored agreement.

January work uses available Artemis PRO displays and a stable software implementation of the graphics API. Supply 64 KiB/Color Pro engineering samples and mouse prototypes when qualified; do not make January work depend on the June professional hardware.

Around June 1982 deliver the 128 KiB professional card and Logix Mono Pro 17 to the development and QA team, alongside the 64 KiB colour card/Color Pro 14 and mouse. This supersedes the earlier proposed January 17-inch prototype handover.
Release acceptance requires native AIONix/ERA build with reliable floating-point geometry and typed coordinate entry.
Release acceptance requires dual-display driver with colour command/status screen and 800x600 drawing canvas; independent palettes and explicit input focus.
Release acceptance requires explicit CAD mouse integration; standard TUI mouse support alone is insufficient.
Release acceptance requires drawing load/save and DXF exchange tests against the other supported AutoCAD builds.
Release acceptance requires supported pen-plotter output and physical drawing verification.
Release acceptance requires measured RAM, storage, redraw and stability requirements on the qualified configuration; backup/restore and reproducible release build.
Release acceptance requires feature baseline agreed with Autodesk; no automatic import of later AutoCAD dimensioning, object-snap or 3D features.

Comstock joins following release from conflicting Xerox obligations. No Diablo or Xerox intellectual property, customer contract or staff transfers automatically.
Adam promises Comstock 10% of Logix issued shares, fulfilled in the single contributor transfer of 12 October 1978; this is not an additional grant.

agreement.title: Letwin London systems-software appointment and equity
agreement.description: AION Software employs Letwin in London as Director of Systems Software and technical liaison to DRI.

party.role: controlling shareholder consenting to the employee award and recruitment sponsor
employer
systems-software director
CEO approving the role within the company business plan

clauses.statement: Letwin leads AION’s systems-software group: CP/M/TUI interface coordination, runtime libraries, assembler integration, development tools, joint acceptance testing and systems-programmer recruitment. DRI retains its own engineering authority and software rights. He reports to Alex d’Agapeyeff; Alex retains company-wide management authority.

Letwin accepts London as his home base. AION supports the required work permission, relocation, temporary housing, Cambridge engineering visits and scheduled US technical visits. The AIONix team’s later move to California does not relocate Letwin; that team has a separate local lead.

AION Software grants Letwin an option over a fixed number of newly issued ordinary shares equal to 5% of the enlarged share capital after full exercise, calculated against the capital at grant and assuming no intervening capital changes. The fixed option share count equals one nineteenth of pre-award issued shares. The option vests in four equal annual instalments after completed service, first on the recruitment anniversary; unvested rights lapse on departure. Vesting establishes exercisable rights, not completed exercise or issued shares.
clauses.unit: percent of enlarged share capital after full option exercise

clauses.statement: The service period is four years from recruitment. Each completed year vests one quarter of the fixed option award. Exercise and share issuance are separate actions. Subsequent capital changes may dilute the award; it has no automatic percentage protection.
This AION Software grant is Letwin’s equity participation in the leadership plan; he receives no Logix allocation.

Starting from the closing allocation of Adam 70% and former CAP shareholders 30%, full exercise of Letwin’s option yields Adam 66.5%, former CAP shareholders 28.5% collectively and Letwin 5%, absent other capital changes. Alex’s interest remains within the former CAP block. This is a conditional fully exercised allocation, not a claim that vesting or issuance has occurred.
clauses.unit: percent of enlarged shares held by Adam after full exercise

agreement.title: CAP controlling investment, AION Software identity and CEO continuity
agreement.description: Adam, CAP and its participating shareholders sign a controlling-investment agreement. CAP continues as the operating company and adopts the AION Software name at closing. Signature creates commitments; the separate closing milestone establishes the ownership change and leadership arrangements.

party.role: investor, purchaser and incoming non-executive chairman
CAP operating company, renamed AION Software at closing

existing shareholders approving the transaction and conveying the agreed shares

clauses.statement: Adam obtains 70% of voting and economic rights immediately after closing through subscription for new shares and purchase of existing shares. No superior-voting share class is created.
clauses.unit: percent of issued shares at closing

clauses.statement: Former CAP shareholders collectively retain 30% immediately after closing. Alex retains a meaningful personal interest within this block, with individual allocations agreed against the verified share register.
clauses.unit: percent of issued shares at closing

clauses.statement: Adam funds a new-share subscription providing development capital and working capital to the company, plus separate consideration paid to selling shareholders. Amounts and the split require the agreed accounts, valuation and investment schedule; neither company funding nor seller consideration is inferred from the ownership percentages.

Closing requires shareholder consent, verified accounts and ownership, intellectual-property rights, existing corporate commitments, and necessary customer or other change-of-control approvals. The parties settle the subscription and purchase documents and record their completion separately from signature.

CAP continues its operating legal entity as AION Software Ltd, subject to registration of the name. The trading transition may use AION Software, formerly CAP. There is no separately founded Danish software company or acquired Danish subsidiary.

Retain headquarters, contract teams and software development in CAP’s London offices. Coordinate through regular engineering visits with AION Labs in Cambridge; co-operation does not merge the companies or their ownership.

Alex d’Agapeyeff continues as CEO and director, with authority over staffing, organisation, existing customer work and new initiatives within the approved business plan. Adam serves as non-executive chairman. The board retains authority over major financing, acquisitions, strategy and CEO appointment; removal without cause carries agreed severance, without guaranteeing tenure regardless of performance.

The five-member board comprises three Adam nominees and two former-CAP shareholder nominees, including Alex. Minority holders receive regular accounts, information rights and proportionate participation rights in later share issues, subject to the agreed employee award.

Preserve existing customer obligations, specialist teams and commercially sound initiatives. No acquisition-driven redundancies are planned. Allocate customer delivery management separately from the product programme and agree retention arrangements for key staff.

Maintain a separately budgeted product programme for the CP/M TUI API, AION C IDE and Abacus, with provision for application-partner engineering and BPI cooperation in 1977. Continuing CAP work and Alex’s initiatives must preserve the programme’s agreed staffing and delivery commitments. BPI obligations arise only under BPI’s separate agreement.

Approve an initial development budget and recruitment plan separately from seller consideration. Plan initially for 15–25 experienced staff, subject to the actual available team and customer commitments; this planning range is not a claim that those staff have already been hired or released from existing contracts. Review capacity, milestones and funding quarterly.

Existing customer and third-party intellectual-property obligations survive. The investment does not grant rights in CP/M or BPI applications. Define delivery, reuse and licensing rights in the separate partner agreements; retain the company’s compiler, application and reusable-component rights as specified there.

Any later employee award must specify its share source, vesting and dilution. The closing percentages exclude ungranted awards; no undisclosed employee pool or automatic percentage protection is created.
